chapter_text:
CHAPTER 25 -- MEASURES OF CENTRAL TENDENCY

Introduction

When we collect data about a group -- the marks of a class, the daily wages of workers, the heights of plants -- we usually get a long list of numbers. To make sense of such data, we look for a single value that can represent the whole set. This single representative value, around which the observations tend to cluster, is called a MEASURE OF CENTRAL TENDENCY (also called an average). It gives us a quick summary of the data and lets us compare one group with another.

The three most common measures of central tendency are the ARITHMETIC MEAN, the MEDIAN and the MODE. This lesson explains how to compute each of them for ungrouped data (a plain list of observations) and for grouped data (data arranged in a frequency table with class intervals). It also gives the empirical relation connecting the three and guidance on which measure to choose.

25.1 THE ARITHMETIC MEAN

(a) Mean of ungrouped data

The arithmetic mean (usually just called the mean) of a set of observations is the sum of all the observations divided by the number of observations.

   mean = (sum of all observations) / (number of observations)

If the observations are x1, x2, x3, ..., xn, then
   mean = (x1 + x2 + ... + xn) / n = (sum of x) / n.

Example 1: The marks of 5 students are 12, 15, 10, 18, 20.
   sum = 12 + 15 + 10 + 18 + 20 = 75.
   mean = 75 / 5 = 15.

When each value xi occurs with a frequency fi, the mean is
   mean = sum(f*x) / sum(f),
where sum(f) = n, the total number of observations.

Example 2: Marks 10, 20, 30, 40 are obtained by 3, 5, 4, 2 students respectively.
   sum(f) = 3 + 5 + 4 + 2 = 14.
   sum(f*x) = 3*10 + 5*20 + 4*30 + 2*40 = 30 + 100 + 120 + 80 = 330.
   mean = 330 / 14 = 23.57 (approximately).

(b) Mean of grouped data -- the DIRECT METHOD

When data is grouped into class intervals (for example 0-10, 10-20, 20-30, ...), we cannot see the individual values. We assume that every observation in a class is located at the CLASS MARK (the midpoint of the class), where
   class mark x = (lower limit + upper limit) / 2.

The mean is then
   mean = sum(f*x) / sum(f),
where x is the class mark of each class and f is its frequency.

Example 3 (direct method): Consider the frequency table
   Class     Frequency f
   0-10          4
   10-20         6
   20-30         8
   30-40         2
Class marks are 5, 15, 25, 35.
   sum(f) = 4 + 6 + 8 + 2 = 20.
   sum(f*x) = 4*5 + 6*15 + 8*25 + 2*35 = 20 + 90 + 200 + 70 = 380.
   mean = 380 / 20 = 19.

(c) The ASSUMED-MEAN METHOD

When the class marks are large, arithmetic becomes heavy. We pick a convenient value a (called the assumed mean, usually a class mark near the middle) and work with the deviations d = x - a.
   mean = a + sum(f*d) / sum(f).

Using the same table with a = 25:
   d = x - 25 gives -20, -10, 0, 10.
   f*d = 4*(-20) + 6*(-10) + 8*0 + 2*10 = -80 - 60 + 0 + 20 = -120.
   mean = 25 + (-120)/20 = 25 - 6 = 19.
The answer is the same as the direct method, as it must be.

(d) The STEP-DEVIATION METHOD

When all classes have the same width h, we can simplify further by using u = (x - a)/h.
   mean = a + (sum(f*u) / sum(f)) * h.

Using the same table with a = 25 and h = 10:
   u = (x - 25)/10 gives -2, -1, 0, 1.
   f*u = 4*(-2) + 6*(-1) + 8*0 + 2*1 = -8 - 6 + 0 + 2 = -12.
   mean = 25 + (-12/20)*10 = 25 - 6 = 19.
Again the mean is 19. The step-deviation method keeps the numbers small and is the quickest for hand calculation.

(e) Properties of the mean

- The mean uses every observation, so it reflects the whole data set.
- The sum of the deviations of the observations from their mean is zero: sum(x - mean) = 0.
- If a constant is added to every observation, the mean increases by that constant. If every observation is multiplied by a constant, the mean is multiplied by that constant.
- The mean is affected by extreme values (very large or very small observations), which is its main drawback.

25.2 THE MEDIAN

The median is the MIDDLE value of the data when the observations are arranged in order (ascending or descending). It divides the data into two equal halves.

(a) Median of ungrouped data

First arrange the n observations in ascending order.
- If n is ODD, the median is the value of the ((n+1)/2)th observation.
- If n is EVEN, the median is the average of the (n/2)th and the (n/2 + 1)th observations.

Example 4 (odd n): Data 7, 3, 9, 5, 11. Arranged: 3, 5, 7, 9, 11. Here n = 5 (odd), so the median is the (5+1)/2 = 3rd term = 7.

Example 5 (even n): Data 10, 20, 30, 40. Already ordered; n = 4 (even). The median is the average of the 2nd and 3rd terms = (20 + 30)/2 = 25.

(b) Median of grouped data

For a frequency distribution we use
   median = L + ((n/2 - cf) / f) * h,
where
   L  = lower boundary of the median class,
   n  = total frequency = sum(f),
   cf = cumulative frequency of the class just BEFORE the median class,
   f  = frequency of the median class,
   h  = class width.
The MEDIAN CLASS is the class in which the cumulative frequency first reaches or exceeds n/2.

Example 6 (grouped median):
   Class     f     cumulative frequency
   0-10      4          4
   10-20     6          10
   20-30     10         20
   30-40     10         30
Here n = 30, so n/2 = 15. The cumulative frequency first reaches or exceeds 15 in the class 20-30, so that is the median class. For it: L = 20, cf = 10 (the cf before the median class), f = 10, h = 10.
   median = 20 + ((15 - 10)/10)*10 = 20 + 5 = 25.

25.3 THE MODE

The mode is the value that occurs MOST OFTEN in the data -- the observation with the highest frequency.

(a) Mode of ungrouped data

Simply find the observation that appears the greatest number of times.
Example 7: In 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 3, 6 the value 3 appears three times (more than any other), so the mode is 3. A data set can have no mode, one mode, or more than one mode.

(b) Mode of grouped data

For a frequency distribution the mode is computed from the MODAL CLASS (the class with the highest frequency) using
   mode = L + ((f1 - f0) / (2*f1 - f0 - f2)) * h,
where
   L  = lower boundary of the modal class,
   f1 = frequency of the modal class,
   f0 = frequency of the class just before the modal class,
   f2 = frequency of the class just after the modal class,
   h  = class width.

Example 8 (grouped mode):
   Class     f
   0-10      3
   10-20     4
   20-30     10
   30-40     6
The highest frequency is 10, so the modal class is 20-30. For it: L = 20, f1 = 10, f0 = 4, f2 = 6, h = 10.
   mode = 20 + ((10 - 4)/(2*10 - 4 - 6))*10 = 20 + (6/10)*10 = 20 + 6 = 26.

25.4 THE EMPIRICAL RELATION

For a moderately asymmetric (skewed) distribution, the three measures are connected by the empirical relation
   Mode = 3*Median - 2*Mean.

This is handy when two of the three are known. For example, if mean = 25 and median = 27, then
   mode = 3*27 - 2*25 = 81 - 50 = 31.
The relation can also be rearranged: Mean = (3*Median - Mode)/2 and Median = (Mode + 2*Mean)/3.

25.5 CHOOSING AN APPROPRIATE MEASURE

- The MEAN is the best measure when the data is fairly symmetric and has no extreme values, because it uses all the data. It is used for further statistical work.
- The MEDIAN is preferred when the data has extreme values (outliers) or an open-ended class, since it is not affected by extreme values -- for example, average income where a few very high incomes would distort the mean.
- The MODE is used when we want the most typical or most popular value -- for example the most common shoe size sold, or the most frequent marks. It is the only average that can be used for non-numerical (qualitative) data.

SUMMARY

- A measure of central tendency is a single value that represents a whole set of data.
- Mean of ungrouped data = (sum of observations)/n; with frequencies, mean = sum(f*x)/sum(f).
- Mean of grouped data (direct) = sum(f*x)/sum(f), x = class mark. Assumed-mean: mean = a + sum(f*d)/sum(f), d = x - a. Step-deviation: mean = a + (sum(f*u)/sum(f))*h, u = (x - a)/h. All three give the same mean.
- Median of ungrouped data: middle term for odd n; average of the two middle terms for even n. Grouped: median = L + ((n/2 - cf)/f)*h.
- Mode of ungrouped data: the most frequent value. Grouped: mode = L + ((f1 - f0)/(2*f1 - f0 - f2))*h.
- Empirical relation: Mode = 3*Median - 2*Mean.
- Choose the mean for symmetric data, the median when there are outliers, and the mode for the most typical value.

chapter_summary.title: Measures of Central Tendency -- Chapter Summary
chapter_summary.intro: This summary reviews the three measures of central tendency -- mean, median and mode -- for both ungrouped and grouped data. It gives the direct, assumed-mean and step-deviation methods for the mean, the median and mode formulas for grouped data, the empirical relation, and guidance on choosing a measure.

sections.heading: The idea of central tendency
bullets: A measure of central tendency is a single value that represents an entire data set -- the value around which the data clusters.
The three common measures are the arithmetic mean, the median and the mode.
Ungrouped data is a plain list of observations; grouped data is arranged in a frequency table of class intervals.
An average lets us summarise data and compare one group with another.

sections.heading: Arithmetic mean
bullets: For ungrouped data, mean = (sum of all observations)/(number of observations); with frequencies mean = sum(f*x)/sum(f).
For grouped data each observation is taken at the class mark x = (lower limit + upper limit)/2.
Direct method: mean = sum(f*x)/sum(f). Assumed-mean method: mean = a + sum(f*d)/sum(f) with d = x - a.
Step-deviation method (equal class width h): mean = a + (sum(f*u)/sum(f))*h with u = (x - a)/h. All methods give the same mean.
The mean uses every observation but is affected by extreme values.

sections.heading: Median
bullets: The median is the middle value after arranging the data in order; it splits the data into two equal halves.
Ungrouped, odd n: median is the ((n+1)/2)th observation.
Ungrouped, even n: median is the average of the (n/2)th and (n/2 + 1)th observations.
Grouped: median = L + ((n/2 - cf)/f)*h, where the median class is the one whose cumulative frequency first reaches n/2.

sections.heading: Mode
bullets: The mode is the most frequently occurring value in the data.
For ungrouped data, read off the observation with the highest frequency.
For grouped data, mode = L + ((f1 - f0)/(2*f1 - f0 - f2))*h, using the modal class (highest frequency).
The mode is the only measure that can be used for qualitative (non-numerical) data.

sections.heading: Empirical relation and choice
bullets: Empirical relation: Mode = 3*Median - 2*Mean, useful when two of the three are known.
Use the mean for fairly symmetric data with no outliers.
Use the median when the data has extreme values or open-ended classes.
Use the mode when the most typical or popular value is required.

key_takeaways: A measure of central tendency represents a whole data set by a single value.
Mean of ungrouped data = (sum of observations)/n; with frequencies, sum(f*x)/sum(f).
Mean of grouped data can be found by the direct, assumed-mean or step-deviation method -- all give the same result.
Median (grouped) = L + ((n/2 - cf)/f)*h; for ungrouped data it is the middle term (or average of two middle terms).
Mode (grouped) = L + ((f1 - f0)/(2*f1 - f0 - f2))*h; for ungrouped data it is the most frequent value.
Choose the mean for symmetric data, the median when there are outliers, and the mode for the most typical value.

glossary.definition: A single value that represents a whole data set -- the value around which the observations tend to cluster. Also called an average.
The sum of all observations divided by the number of observations; for a frequency distribution, sum(f*x)/sum(f).
The middle value of a data set when the observations are arranged in order; it divides the data into two equal halves.
The value that occurs most frequently in a data set; the observation with the highest frequency.
Data presented as a plain list of individual observations, not organised into class intervals.
Data organised into class intervals with their frequencies in a frequency distribution table.
The midpoint of a class interval, equal to (lower limit + upper limit)/2; used as the representative x-value of the class.
The number of observations that fall in a particular class or take a particular value.
The running total of frequencies up to and including a given class.
The class interval in which the cumulative frequency first reaches or exceeds n/2.
The class interval with the highest frequency, used in the grouped-mode formula.
A convenient value a (often a central class mark) chosen to simplify mean calculation via deviations d = x - a.
The quantity u = (x - a)/h used to simplify the mean calculation when all classes have equal width h.
The approximate relationship Mode = 3*Median - 2*Mean, valid for moderately skewed distributions.
The size of a class interval, h = upper limit - lower limit.

worksheet.title: Worksheet -- Measures of Central Tendency
worksheet.instructions: Attempt all questions. Show full working for every computation. Use the formulas for grouped mean, median and mode where a frequency table is given.

questions.question: Define a measure of central tendency and name the three common measures. State one situation in which the median is preferred to the mean.
questions.answer: A measure of central tendency is a single value that represents a whole data set -- the value around which the observations tend to cluster (an average). The three common measures are the arithmetic MEAN, the MEDIAN and the MODE. The median is preferred to the mean when the data contains extreme values (outliers) or an open-ended class -- for example average income, where a few very large incomes would pull the mean up but leave the median unaffected.
questions.explanation: Definition + the three measures + when to prefer the median.

questions.question: Find the mean of the following distribution by the DIRECT method. Classes 0-10, 10-20, 20-30, 30-40 with frequencies 4, 6, 8, 2.
questions.explanation: Direct method: mean = sum(f*x)/sum(f) with x = class mark.

questions.question: For the same distribution (0-10:4, 10-20:6, 20-30:8, 30-40:2) find the mean by the ASSUMED-MEAN method and by the STEP-DEVIATION method, taking assumed mean a = 25.
questions.answer:
Class marks x = 5, 15, 25, 35; frequencies f = 4, 6, 8, 2; sum(f) = 20; h = 10.
Assumed-mean method (d = x - a, a = 25): d = -20, -10, 0, 10.
  f*d = 4*(-20) + 6*(-10) + 8*0 + 2*10 = -80 - 60 + 0 + 20 = -120.
  mean = a + sum(f*d)/sum(f) = 25 + (-120)/20 = 25 - 6 = 19.
Step-deviation method (u = (x - a)/h): u = -2, -1, 0, 1.
  f*u = 4*(-2) + 6*(-1) + 8*0 + 2*1 = -8 - 6 + 0 + 2 = -12.
  mean = a + (sum(f*u)/sum(f))*h = 25 + (-12/20)*10 = 25 - 6 = 19.
Both methods give mean = 19, agreeing with the direct method.

questions.question: Find the MEDIAN of the distribution: 0-10:4, 10-20:6, 20-30:10, 30-40:10.
questions.answer:
Build cumulative frequencies: 0-10 -> 4; 10-20 -> 10; 20-30 -> 20; 30-40 -> 30. So n = 30 and n/2 = 15.
The cumulative frequency first reaches or exceeds 15 in the class 20-30, so the median class is 20-30.
For it: L = 20, cf = 10 (cf before the median class), f = 10, h = 10.
median = L + ((n/2 - cf)/f)*h = 20 + ((15 - 10)/10)*10 = 20 + 5 = 25.
questions.explanation: Grouped median formula; median class where cf reaches n/2 = 15.

questions.question: Find the MODE of the distribution: 0-10:3, 10-20:4, 20-30:10, 30-40:6.
questions.answer:
The highest frequency is 10, so the modal class is 20-30.
For it: L = 20, f1 = 10 (modal class frequency), f0 = 4 (class before), f2 = 6 (class after), h = 10.
mode = L + ((f1 - f0)/(2*f1 - f0 - f2))*h = 20 + ((10 - 4)/(20 - 4 - 6))*10 = 20 + (6/10)*10 = 20 + 6 = 26.
questions.explanation: Grouped mode formula with modal class 20-30.

questions.question: For a distribution the mean is 25 and the median is 27. Use the empirical relation to find the mode.
questions.answer: Empirical relation: Mode = 3*Median - 2*Mean = 3*27 - 2*25 = 81 - 50 = 31. So the mode is 31.

questions.question: Find the mean of the ungrouped data 12, 15, 10, 18, 20.
questions.answer: sum = 12 + 15 + 10 + 18 + 20 = 75. Number of observations n = 5. mean = 75/5 = 15.

questions.question: Find the median of the ungrouped data 10, 20, 30, 40.
questions.answer: The data is already in ascending order and n = 4 (even). The two middle terms are the 2nd and 3rd terms, 20 and 30. median = (20 + 30)/2 = 25.
questions.explanation: Even n: average of the two middle terms.

questions.question: Find the mode of the ungrouped data 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 3, 6.
questions.answer: Count how often each value occurs: 2 once, 3 three times, 4 once, 5 once, 6 once. The value 3 occurs most often, so the mode is 3.

questions.question: The monthly incomes (in thousands) of the 9 workers in a small firm are 8, 9, 9, 10, 11, 12, 12, 13, 90. (a) Find the mean and the median. (b) Which measure better represents a typical income here, and why?
questions.answer:
(a) sum = 8 + 9 + 9 + 10 + 11 + 12 + 12 + 13 + 90 = 174. n = 9, so mean = 174/9 = 19.33 (thousand). For the median, the data is already ordered; n = 9 (odd), so median is the (9+1)/2 = 5th term = 11 (thousand).
(b) The MEDIAN (11 thousand) better represents a typical income. The single very large value 90 is an outlier that pulls the mean up to 19.33, which is higher than 8 of the 9 incomes and so is not typical. The median is not affected by the extreme value, so it is the more representative measure here.
questions.explanation: Outlier inflates the mean; median is the better representative.

questions.question: A single value that represents a whole data set is called a measure of ____ tendency.
The mean of 6, 8, 10, 12 is ____.
For a frequency distribution the mean equals sum(f*x) divided by ____.
The class mark of the interval 30-40 is ____.
For 0-10:4, 10-20:6, 20-30:8, 30-40:2 the mean by the direct method is ____.
In the step-deviation method u = (x - a)/____.
In the assumed-mean method the deviation is d = x - ____.
The median of 3, 5, 7, 9, 11 is ____.
In the grouped median formula median = L + ((n/2 - cf)/f)*h, the symbol cf is the ____ frequency of the class before the median class.
The median of 4, 6, 8, 10 is ____.
In the mode formula, f1 is the frequency of the ____ class.
The empirical relation is Mode = 3*Median - 2*____.
If mean = 20 and median = 22, then mode = ____.
When data contains extreme values, the ____ is the best measure of central tendency.
What is a measure of central tendency? Name the three common ones.
questions.answer: A measure of central tendency is a single value that represents a whole data set -- the value around which the observations tend to cluster (an average). The three common measures are the arithmetic mean, the median and the mode.

questions.question: Distinguish between ungrouped and grouped data.
questions.answer: Ungrouped data is a plain list of individual observations, e.g. 5, 8, 12, 15. Grouped data is arranged into class intervals with their frequencies in a table, e.g. 0-10: 4, 10-20: 6, 20-30: 8. Grouped data hides individual values, so we use class marks to represent them.

questions.question: Find the mean of 4, 6, 8, 10, 12.
questions.answer: sum = 4 + 6 + 8 + 10 + 12 = 40. Number of observations n = 5. mean = 40/5 = 8.

questions.question: Find the mean of 15, 18, 21, 24, 27.
The values 10, 20, 30 occur with frequencies 2, 3, 5. Find the mean.
The mean of 5 numbers is 14. If four of them are 10, 12, 15, 18, find the fifth.
questions.answer: Total sum = mean * n = 14*5 = 70. Sum of the four known numbers = 10 + 12 + 15 + 18 = 55. Fifth number = 70 - 55 = 15.

questions.question: The mean of 8 observations is 12. If each observation is increased by 5, what is the new mean?
questions.answer: Adding a constant to every observation increases the mean by that constant. New mean = 12 + 5 = 17.

questions.question: Find the mean of the distribution 0-10:4, 10-20:6, 20-30:8, 30-40:2 by the direct method.
Find the mean of 10-20:3, 20-30:5, 30-40:2 by the direct method.
Find the class marks of the intervals 0-10, 10-20, 20-30, 30-40.
Find the mean of 0-10:4, 10-20:6, 20-30:8, 30-40:2 by the assumed-mean method, taking a = 25.
Find the mean of 0-10:4, 10-20:6, 20-30:8, 30-40:2 by the step-deviation method (a = 25, h = 10).
Why do the direct, assumed-mean and step-deviation methods give the same mean?
questions.answer: All three are algebraically equivalent ways of computing sum(f*x)/sum(f). The assumed-mean and step-deviation methods just shift and rescale the x-values to make the arithmetic easier (using d = x - a or u = (x - a)/h), but the shift and scale are reversed at the end by adding a and multiplying by h. So the final mean is identical.
questions.explanation: They are the same formula rewritten.

questions.question: Find the median of 12, 7, 15, 9, 20.
questions.answer: Arrange in order: 7, 9, 12, 15, 20. n = 5 (odd), so the median is the (5+1)/2 = 3rd term = 12.

questions.question: Find the median of 4, 8, 6, 10, 12, 2.
questions.answer: Arrange in order: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10, 12. n = 6 (even), so the median is the average of the 3rd and 4th terms = (6 + 8)/2 = 7.
questions.explanation: Even n: average of two middle terms.

questions.question: Find the median of the distribution 0-10:4, 10-20:6, 20-30:10, 30-40:10.
questions.answer: Cumulative frequencies: 4, 10, 20, 30. n = 30, n/2 = 15. The median class is 20-30 (cf first reaches 15 there). L = 20, cf = 10, f = 10, h = 10. median = 20 + ((15 - 10)/10)*10 = 20 + 5 = 25.

questions.question: Find the median of 0-10:5, 10-20:10, 20-30:20, 30-40:5.
questions.answer: Cumulative frequencies: 5, 15, 35, 40. n = 40, n/2 = 20. The median class is 20-30 (cf reaches 20 there). L = 20, cf = 15, f = 20, h = 10. median = 20 + ((20 - 15)/20)*10 = 20 + 2.5 = 22.5.

questions.question: Write the formula for the median of grouped data and name each symbol.
questions.answer: median = L + ((n/2 - cf)/f)*h, where L is the lower boundary of the median class, n is the total frequency, cf is the cumulative frequency of the class before the median class, f is the frequency of the median class, and h is the class width.

questions.question: Find the mode of 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 6, 9.
questions.answer: Count each value: 6 occurs three times, more than any other value. So the mode is 6.

questions.question: Find the mode of 10, 12, 12, 13, 15, 15, 15, 18.
questions.answer: The value 15 occurs three times, more than any other. So the mode is 15.

questions.question: Find the mode of the distribution 0-10:3, 10-20:4, 20-30:10, 30-40:6.
Write the formula for the mode of grouped data and name f1, f0, f2.
questions.answer: mode = L + ((f1 - f0)/(2*f1 - f0 - f2))*h, where f1 is the frequency of the modal class, f0 is the frequency of the class just before it, f2 is the frequency of the class just after it, L is the lower boundary of the modal class and h is the class width.

questions.question: If mean = 20 and median = 22, find the mode using the empirical relation.
If mode = 12 and median = 15, find the mean.
questions.answer: From Mode = 3*Median - 2*Mean, we get Mean = (3*Median - Mode)/2 = (3*15 - 12)/2 = (45 - 12)/2 = 33/2 = 16.5.

questions.question: If mean = 11 and mode = 8, find the median.
The daily wages of 7 workers are 300, 310, 320, 330, 340, 350, 2000 rupees. Which measure of central tendency best represents a typical wage, and why?
questions.answer: The MEDIAN best represents a typical wage. Arranged in order the median is the 4th of 7 values = 330. The single very large wage 2000 is an outlier that would pull the mean far above most workers' wages (mean = 3950/7 = 564), making it unrepresentative. The median 330 is unaffected by the outlier and reflects a typical wage.

questions.question: State one situation each where the mean, the median and the mode is the most suitable measure.
questions.answer: Mean: symmetric data with no outliers, e.g. average marks of a class. Median: data with extreme values or open-ended classes, e.g. average income. Mode: the most typical or popular value, e.g. the most common shoe size sold.

questions.question: Why is the mode the only measure of central tendency that can be used for qualitative data such as favourite colours?
questions.answer: The mean and median require the data to be numerical, because they involve arithmetic (adding, dividing) or ordering by size. Qualitative data such as favourite colours cannot be added or ranked meaningfully. The mode, however, only requires counting how often each category occurs, so it can identify the most frequent category (e.g. the most popular colour). Hence the mode is the only measure applicable to qualitative data.
questions.explanation: Mode needs only counting, not arithmetic.

questions.question: For the distribution 10-20:5, 20-30:12, 30-40:8, find the mode.

Read the passage and answer the questions.

A teacher recorded the marks (out of 10) of 8 students: 6, 7, 5, 8, 6, 9, 7, 8.

(i) Find the sum of the marks.
(ii) How many observations are there?
(iii) Find the mean mark.
(iv) State one drawback of the mean as a measure.
questions.answer:
(i) sum = 6 + 7 + 5 + 8 + 6 + 9 + 7 + 8 = 56.
(ii) There are n = 8 observations.
(iii) mean = 56/8 = 7.
(iv) Drawback: the mean is affected by extreme values (a single very large or very small mark would distort it).
questions.explanation: Ungrouped mean from a small data set.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The heights (in cm) of plants are grouped as: 0-10 (frequency 4), 10-20 (frequency 6), 20-30 (frequency 8), 30-40 (frequency 2).

(i) Write the class marks.
(ii) Find sum(f).
(iii) Find sum(f*x).
(iv) Find the mean by the direct method.

Read the passage and answer the questions.

For the distribution 0-10:4, 10-20:6, 20-30:8, 30-40:2 an assumed mean a = 25 and class width h = 10 are chosen.

(i) Write the deviations d = x - a.
(ii) Find sum(f*d) and hence the mean by the assumed-mean method.
(iii) Write the step deviations u = (x - a)/h.
(iv) Find the mean by the step-deviation method.

Read the passage and answer the questions.

The distribution of daily wages is 0-10:4, 10-20:6, 20-30:10, 30-40:10.

(i) Write the cumulative frequencies.
(ii) Find n and n/2.
(iii) Identify the median class.
(iv) Find the median.
questions.answer:
(i) Cumulative frequencies: 4, 10, 20, 30.
(ii) n = 30, so n/2 = 15.
(iii) The cumulative frequency first reaches 15 in the class 20-30, so the median class is 20-30.
(iv) L = 20, cf = 10, f = 10, h = 10. median = 20 + ((15 - 10)/10)*10 = 20 + 5 = 25.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The distribution of shoe sizes sold is 0-10:3, 10-20:4, 20-30:10, 30-40:6.

(i) Identify the modal class.
(ii) Write f1, f0 and f2.
(iii) Find the mode.
(iv) Why is the mode a suitable measure here?
questions.answer:
(i) The highest frequency is 10, so the modal class is 20-30.
(ii) f1 = 10 (modal class), f0 = 4 (class before), f2 = 6 (class after).
(iii) mode = 20 + ((10 - 4)/(2*10 - 4 - 6))*10 = 20 + (6/10)*10 = 20 + 6 = 26.
(iv) The mode is suitable because a shopkeeper wants the most commonly sold (most popular) size, which is exactly what the mode identifies.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

For a certain distribution the mean is 24 and the median is 26.

(i) State the empirical relation.
(ii) Find the mode.
(iii) If instead the mode were 20 and mean 24, find the median.
(iv) Why is the relation called 'empirical'?
questions.answer:
(i) Empirical relation: Mode = 3*Median - 2*Mean.
(ii) Mode = 3*26 - 2*24 = 78 - 48 = 30.
(iii) Median = (Mode + 2*Mean)/3 = (20 + 48)/3 = 68/3 = 22.67 (approximately).
(iv) It is called empirical because it is an approximate relationship observed to hold for moderately skewed distributions, rather than an exact algebraic identity.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The monthly salaries (in thousands) of 6 employees are 12, 14, 15, 16, 18, 90.

(i) Find the mean.
(ii) Find the median.
(iii) Which value is an outlier?
(iv) Which measure better represents a typical salary, and why?
questions.answer:
(i) sum = 12 + 14 + 15 + 16 + 18 + 90 = 165. mean = 165/6 = 27.5 (thousand).
(ii) Ordered data; n = 6 (even); median = (15 + 16)/2 = 15.5 (thousand).
(iii) The value 90 is an outlier (far larger than the others).
(iv) The median (15.5) better represents a typical salary. The outlier 90 pulls the mean up to 27.5, higher than 5 of the 6 salaries, so the mean is misleading; the median is unaffected by the outlier.
questions.explanation: Outlier makes median the better measure.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The number of goals scored by a team in 10 matches is 0, 1, 2, 2, 3, 1, 2, 4, 2, 3.

(i) Find the total number of goals.
(ii) Find the mean goals per match.
(iii) Find the mode of the data.
(iv) Find the median of the data.
questions.answer:
(i) Total = 0 + 1 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 + 2 + 4 + 2 + 3 = 20 goals.
(ii) mean = 20/10 = 2 goals per match.
(iii) The value 2 occurs four times, more than any other, so the mode is 2.
(iv) Ordered: 0, 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 4. n = 10 (even); median = average of 5th and 6th terms = (2 + 2)/2 = 2.
questions.explanation: Mean, mode and median of the same small data set.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

The marks of a class are grouped as 0-10:5, 10-20:10, 20-30:20, 30-40:5.

(i) Write the cumulative frequencies.
(ii) Identify the median class.
(iii) Find the median.
(iv) Find the class mark of the median class.
questions.answer:
(i) Cumulative frequencies: 5, 15, 35, 40. n = 40, n/2 = 20.
(ii) The cumulative frequency first reaches 20 in the class 20-30, so the median class is 20-30.
(iii) L = 20, cf = 15, f = 20, h = 10. median = 20 + ((20 - 15)/20)*10 = 20 + 2.5 = 22.5.
(iv) Class mark of 20-30 = (20 + 30)/2 = 25.

questions.question:
Read the passage and answer the questions.

A survey of the ages (in years) of members gives 0-20:2, 20-40:3, 40-60:5.

(i) Write the class marks.
(ii) Find sum(f) and sum(f*x).
(iii) Find the mean age by the direct method.
(iv) Verify using the step-deviation method with a = 30, h = 20.
